2000 CanLII 21370 (CA IRB)
- 1 - M99-10099 
 These are the reasons for decision with respect to the refugee claim made by Madam XXXXXXXXXXXXX. The claimant is a citizen of Lebanon who has alleged that she has a well-founded fear of persecution in Lebanon by reason of her membership in a particular social group, namely as a woman subjected to domestic violence. 
ALLEGED FACTS 
 The claimant, who was 47 years old at the time of the hearing, was born in Beirut, in Lebanon. She has six years of education and has 30 years of work experience. She has worked as a seamst ress, salesperson and a cleaning lady. It was in February 1998 that she met and began to keep company with XXXXXXXXX who was a customer of XXXXX, the store where the claimant was working as a salesperson. In May 1998, Mr. XXXX proposed that she leave her employment and live with him. In spite of pressure from her family, who did not want her to keep company with a Moslem since she was a Christian, the claimant decided to live with Mr. XXXX in the town of XXXXXX. Some months later, Mr. XXXX began to be aggres sive and violent towards her. He beat her, threatened to kill her, locked her in the house, and subsequently forced her to wear the hijab. In November 1998, he told her that she had to work and give him the money. The claimant then worked in pr ivate homes as a cleaning lady and gave him the money. Mr. XXXX spent all of the money with his friends and continued to behave aggressively toward the claimant . It was in June 1999 that the claimant decided to escape to a friend’s place for th ree weeks. She also went to see her family, but they refused to receive her. After having left Mr. XXXX in June 1999 and having attempted to take refuge with her parents, she contacted the Lebanese authorities in order to obtain their protec tion. At the police station in Beirut, she was informed that they could not help her since this was a domestic matter and that she should go to the religious author ities. Following this, she went to the Armenian Church, but all help was refused her since she was not married and her spouse was a Moslem. The mother of the claimant had come to Canada and was staying with her brothers. The claimant therefore began to take steps to come to Canada in order to join her brothers and her mother. XXXX ver, her application for a Canadian visa was refused. She therefore decided to come via the United States with the goal of eventually entering Canada. The claimant left Lebanon on XXXXX, 1998. She arrived the next day in Detroit, Michiga n, in the United States, where she stayed 
2000 CanLII 21370 (CA IRB)
- 2 - M99-10099 
 until XXXXX, 1999. She went to Windsor that same day, where she claimed refugee status. She left Windsor on Oc tober 20, 1999 and came to Montréal to join her family. 
ANALYSIS 
 The evidence presented by the claima nt, her counsel and the refugee claim officer (RCO) consists essentially of the claimant's testimony, her Personal Information Form (PIF), personal docu ments and the documentary evidence concerning the socio-political situation in Lebanon. As well as this evidence, the panel read the Chairperson's guidelines concerning women refugee claimants who fear persecution by reason of their gender. The analysis of all of the evidence su bmitted leads us to conclude that the claimant, who says that she fears being persecuted because of her gender, as a woman subjected to domestic violence, has not discharged the burden of proof which rests on her to demonstrate a serious possibility of persecution based on one of the five Convention grounds should she return to Lebanon. The panel has analyzed and assessed the credibility of the claimant. Her testimony was riddled with discrepancies, omissions, alterations and vagueness. The panel finds that the claimant was not a credible witness. The claimant testified that she had met Mr. XXXX in February 1998 and that they had kept company until May 1998; then she had decided to live with him. The abuse began in August 1998, and it was in September 1998 that she expressed her intention to leave him. Sh e was finally able to escape in June 1999. The claimant testified that she is afraid that Mr. XXXX will kill her if she returns to Lebanon and that she has feared for he r life since October 1998. She testified that she has had no news from Lebanon si nce her departure, since she does not communicate with her sister. The panel asked the claimant seve ral questions regarding Mr. XXXX in order to better understand the man. The re sponses of the claimant on this subject were very evasive and general and lacking in details that were satisfactory to the panel. For example, she testified in a very general way that she did not know what kind of work Mr. XXXX did and th at she had not asked him during the entire period that they were together. The panel asked her if Mr. XXXX was the owner of the house where they were stay ing. She again responded that she did not know. She also testified that she kne w nothing about his family. The panel 
2000 CanLII 21370 (CA IRB)
- 3 - M99-10099 
 seriously questions the plausibility of this total lack of information about this individual who was a big mystery in the life of the claimant. Towards the end of the hearing, howev er, when her counsel asked her to talk about Mr. XXXX, the claimant descri bed him as a man who carried a weapon and who could probably have been a memb er of the Hezbollah, a Moslem party with a militant wing. When the panel as ked her why she never mentioned this when the RCO and the members of the pane l were questioning her, she said that she had just remembered it. The panel re jects her explanation, which it does not believe. We find that she was merely tailoring her testimony for the purpose of embellishing it. The claimant testified that she never consulted a doctor and did not have to be hospitalized in connection with the abuse that was inflicted on her. The claimant stated that it was in June 1999 th at she decided to leave him. The panel asked her when she had announced to him th at she intended to leave him. She once again gave inconsistent answers; fi rst she said it was in November 1998 and later she changed her testimony to say th at it was in September 1998. The panel has drawn a negative inference from th ese changes, and this undermined her credibility. The claimant testified that Mr. XXXX had persuaded her to leave her employment after 30 years of service a nd she was without work until November 1998, when Mr. XXXX found her a job as clea ning lady. The panel asked her in which neighbourhood she did this work. Sh e again answered evasively that she did not know. The panel confronted her w ith her statement that she had lived for 40 years in Beirut and that she should th erefore have an idea of the names of the neighbourhoods. She responded that ther e was a war going on and that people were not able to move around freely. The panel rejected her explanations and firmly believes that in a city like Beirut , where she claimed to have lived for 40 years, she would have been able nonethele ss to at least direct the panel to the neighbourhoods where she had allegedly worked as a cleaning lady. The panel asked her if she could live in Beirut, and she answered that she could not because he would kill her. When she was asked to explain how he would know that she was in Lebanon, she answered quite briefly that if anyone wanted to find out, he would find out. The panel confronted her with the fact that from June 1999 until her departure in October 1999, Mr. XXXX had not found her in Beirut and with the question why it is that he would be interested in finding 
2000 CanLII 21370 (CA IRB)
- 4 - M99-10099 
 her more than a year after her departure. At that point, the claimant changed her response, saying that Mr. XXXX had looked for but had not found her. The panel asked the claimant why she had not men tioned that in her PIF. She responded quite simply that she had not remembered this fact. The panel rejects these explanations and believes that she wa s once again tailoring her answers to embellish her testimony; it does not find her credible concerning this central element of her claim. When she was as ked how she knew this, she was unable to provide an answer. When the question was put to her a second time, she modified her testimony, saying that he had turned up at her sister’s place. The panel has drawn a negative inference from all of thes e omissions and alterations. First, she alleged that she did not communicate with her sister and then, that she would have known through her sister that Mr. XXXX had been looking for her. These discrepancies and alterations in her testimony completely undermine her credibility. Towards the end of the hearing wh en her counsel asked her how Mr. XXXX would be able to find her in Lebanon, she modified her testimony once again, saying that he had taken her photogr aph one day and told her that he was doing it so as to be able to find her. Th e panel does not believe this allegation by the claimant in the least. The claimant had never mentioned this before, either in her PIF or in her testimony, until the end of her hearing, when she was responding to questions by her counsel. We belie ve that she was once again tailoring her testimony merely to embellish her story. The panel asked her to explain for what purpose she had received a copy of the family register (P-3)
1 in May 1999. The claimant answered that it was because Mr. XXXX had asked her to obtai n this document in case they got married. Subsequently, the claimant ch anged her testimony, saying that she had obtained it for the purpose of getting her passp ort. She explained that the identity card, the personal record and all of the relevant documents had been obtained for the purpose of a possible marriage. It is noted that the identity card was issued on XXXXXX, 1999, a time when the claimant had left or was preparing to leave. The panel seriously questions the plausi bility of this statement, which is inconsistent with her earlier statements concerning her fear. On one hand, she alleged that she was suffering and that Mr. XXXX was abusing her physically and on the other hand, that she was gathering these documents in case of marriage. The claimant testified that she had b een shut up in the house of a friend in a suburb of Beirut for several months. The panel asked her to explain how she 
2000 CanLII 21370 (CA IRB)
- 5 - M99-10099 
 had been able to take the necessary steps to obtain her passport, an American visa and her identity card. The claimant then admitted that she had gone out several times in order to make preparations for leaving Lebanon and that she had had to go out to obtain her passport, her identity card and an American visa, for which she travelled to Syria. The panel again notes the discrepancies and alterations in the claimant’s testimony, and once ag ain, this tainted her credibility. When her counsel asked whether the Hezbollah were looking for her, she answered that she did not know and that everyone in this region has a beard and the women wear veils. The panel notes again the inconsistent responses of the claimant. On one hand, she testified that she did not know this part of the city well and on the other hand, she stated in re sponse to questions by her counsel, that it is a region overrun with Hezbollah. These discrepancies undermined her credibility. After her application for a Canadian visa had been refused, the claimant applied for an American visa since she had a cousin and an uncle in the United States. She explained that the applica tion for an American visa was for the purpose of helping her to obtain a Canadi an visa. The panel asked her why she had not claimed refugee status during her stay in the United States. She replied that her relatives had not helped her and that she did not know the language; therefore, she had been unable to take th e necessary steps. Later in her testimony, she changed her answer, saying that she ha d asked her cousin, but that he had not wanted to help her. The panel asked he r to explain how, when she could not get information in the United States on how to claim refugee status since she did not speak English, she was able to do so in Wi ndsor, Ontario. She testified that it was the taxi driver who had driven her to Windsor who helped her. The panel asked her why this same driver was not able to help her in the United States. She changed her answer and said that she t hought that it would be better if she were with her family. The panel has drawn a negative inference from all of these changes in her responses and questioned he r subjective fear, considering the delay in making a claim, since she had passed th rough a country which is a signatory to the Convention. The claimant testified that she had as ked the police for help, as well as her church in Lebanon, but without any success. The documentary evidence
2 reports that in Lebanon there is legal aid for vi ctims of violence as well as Lebanese associations that have existed since 1994 to combat violence against women. 
2000 CanLII 21370 (CA IRB)
- 6 - M99-10099 
 After having examined the evidence, the testimony as well as the documentary evidence, that was submitted to it, the panel finds that the evidence is not sufficient to establish that there is a reasonable chance that the claimant would be persecuted within the meaning of Adjei
3 if she returned to her country of origin. Moreover, in view of the preceding evidence and such a general lack of credibility, we have no other choice but to find the whole of the claimant’s testimony to be lacking in credibility. Th e words of Mr. Justice XXXXXXXXX in the Sheikh
4 case are directly applicable to the case in point: […] [E]ven without disbelieving every word an applicant has uttered, a [panel] may reasonably find him so lacking in credibility that it concludes there is no credible evidence relevant to his claim […] In other words, a general finding of a lack of credibility on the part of the applicant may conceivably extend to all relevant evidence emanating from his testimony. 
CONCLUSION 
 For these reasons, the panel concludes that the claimant, Madam XXXXXXXXXXXXX, is not a “Convention refugee” under section 2(1) of the Immigration Act. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX
